summary:
Project WATS turns SPHEREx spectral images of a sky patch into a living instrument: spectra, light curves, source extraction, annotations, collections, activity, moving-object candidates, and export. It queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for public SPHEREx Level 2 observations, downloads IBE cutouts, reprojects them onto a common north-up grid, and renders gray and color frames directly in the browser.

No accounts. No API keys. Just the sky, freely given
details:
Project WATS — Where Astronomical Targets Shimmer

Project WATS started with a simple frustration: infrared sky data should be easy to look at, and for most people it simply is not. So we built a web based blink comparator for the SPHEREx era. Old school astronomers used to flick two photographic plates back and forth to catch a moving or variable object. My app brings that trick to the browser, using public SPHEREx Level 2 infrared observations, and lets anyone study how a patch of sky changes across time and wavelength.

The idea is straightforward. You type in coordinates or pick a preset, and my backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA's TAP service to find SPHEREx detector frames covering your target in the selected data release. It then pulls FITS cutouts on demand through the IRSA cutout service, with caching and fallbacks, reprojects everything onto a common north up grid, and hands you clean, browser ready frames. From there you can blink, subtract, sum, and compare bands, extract spectra on the fly, view light curves, check quality and completeness, and overlay catalogs like CatWISE2020 and Gaia DR3. Every view lives behind a shareable URL, so a finding is never stuck on one screen.

Everything runs on a Flask backend with Python, astropy, numpy, scipy, and Pillow, while the frontend is unbundled ES modules drawing on Canvas 2D, helped by three.js, deck.gl, OpenSeadragon, and uPlot. No accounts, no API keys, no special software.

I host it on the free tier of PythonAnywhere, a choice I made deliberately. It is constrained and occasionally stubborn, but keeping the project open and reachable matters more to me right now than raw power. The vision is long term. During development IRSA itself went down, which slowed live testing, yet that only reinforced a lesson the sky keeps teaching, build patiently, cache what you can, and let the data shine when it arrives.

The User Manual is present at (https://github.com/MDSUWasi/Project-WATS/blob/master/USER_MANUAL.md)

The Repository is available at (https://github.com/MDSUWasi/Project-WATS)
